chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Where music is going and the businessmen's 'new gimmick'
summary: Wilson reads trade-paper news of slumping fad music and predicts businessmen will take any new electronics and sell it as a gimmick, while art survives.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well, where do you think it's going, Teddy? Music and jazz.
Well, like this Variety magazine says, the fad music has taken a big dive now, the stuff that sells
gold, a million records -- that whole world has taken a dive, but the jazz is just staying on that same keel, the symphony is staying on the same keel, the classical is staying on that same keel.

So along with that big pop thing is an artistic level that just goes its own way, and I just hope more people get into that, and it may be that if that artisitic type of music will pick up a big audience now. Where can the gimmick people go now? They'll run out of it -- they'll slow down, as the thing says -- all these record companies are laying off employees, one laid off 1,000 employees. These companies that have been selling (CUT)
So, Teddy, we been talking about the future of music and what's been happening. I say where do you think it's going; but of course I don't know, and you don't either.

Unless they come through with another gimmick -- with this new development of electronics, like I was saying about these new games they have for the kids, electronic world, there's no telling what it will open up, and the only thing is when the businessmen take hold of it, it will be the same old thing all over again. They will control the public taste, the exposure to what is available, and they will control the production of it and the publicizing of it and the marketing of it -- just like they do with the rock and roll records now that they have trouble selling.

That sort of has run its course, but when they think of a new gimmick, you see, the whole thing is a new gimmick all along to -- like the dubbing of the rock rhythms, like I said earlier, rhythm section rock underneath a string section of the New York Philharmonic, and they're making, just doing horrible things that no musician would ever dream of doing. But the businessmen will do it to try to create some public interest in order to make a buck. A businessman will do anything for a buck, see. That's the law of the jungle.
What happens when you're not a businessman? A musician is so busy creating, developing his talent, that we would probably be playing with bows and arrows if it hadn't been for the businessmen.

But the strength of the musician is something that no man understands -- underneath the whole structure of what we're talking about with the businessman, there's something that keeps the audience alive and always has, from Michaelangelo's time right on to now. There are people who are artistic and who survive, in spite of the businessman.
The businessman who's only concerned with a new gimmick to sell to make a buck, and after that runs its course, thinks of something else new, like changing the
label on the thing -- like if you don't change the product, then put a new label on it, put on there "NEW!" Economy size, It's the same old stuff, see. New, advanced economy sized!
